citation.title: Machine learning for topology optimization: Physics-based learning through an independent training strategy
citation.authors: Fernando V. Senhora, Heng Chi, Yuyu Zhang, Lucia Mirabella, Tsz Ling Elaine Tang, Glaucio H. Paulino
citation.venue: Computer Methods in Applied Mechanics and Engineering 398, 115116
citation.version_coded: version of record at author institutional site

claim.primary_outcome_paraphrase: An independently trained CNN that predicts fine-mesh sensitivities makes topology optimization up to 30 times faster than conventional fine-mesh optimization, with similar accuracy.
claim.claimed_speedup_basis: Abstract states up to 30×; Section 6.4 and Figure 16 report a measured maximum of 26.5× for the 10-million-element MBB problem, rounded in the abstract.
claim.alternatives: Section 6.4 reports 26.5× for 10 million elements; Introduction compares about 27× with about 10× in a prior ML method.

baseline.classical_method: Standard SIMP density topology optimization with fine-resolution FEA at every iteration (Sections 3, 6.4)
baseline.implementation: In-house C++/CUDA FEA, Python 3.6 optimization and PyTorch ML (Section 6)
baseline.hardware_classical: 24 Intel Xeon CPUs, 251 GB RAM, NVIDIA Titan Xp GPU with 12 GB RAM for FEA (Section 6.4)
baseline.hardware_ml: Same machine; one NVIDIA Titan Xp GPU for ML prediction and one for FEA (Section 6.4)
baseline.problem_size: 1-million- and 10-million-element 3D MBB meshes for timing; 38,016,000-element bridge solved only by ML (Sections 6.3–6.4)
baseline.classical_iterations: Maximum 200, SIMP and Heaviside continuation schedule given (Section 6)
baseline.classical_time: Figure 16 gives plotted runtimes for 1-million- and 10-million-element MBB cases; exact numeric wall times not printed in extracted text (Section 6.4)
baseline.ml_time: 18 hours for 38,016,000-element bridge; Figure 16 plots runtimes of 1-million- and 10-million-element MBB cases (Sections 6.3–6.4)
baseline.data_generation_cost: Four conventional TO training problems at 165,888, 221,184, 262,144 and 186,624 fine elements; time not stated (Section 6.1)
baseline.quality_metric: Compliance and volume fraction of final designs; reference compliance from standard TO (Figures 12–13, Section 6.2)
baseline.quality_gap: For 1,327,104-element MBB cases, compliance lies within 1.5% of reference (Section 6.2); fine-mesh compliance for 38,016,000-element bridge cannot be calculated and is estimated from coarse mesh (Section 6.3)

R1.evidence: Abstract claims 30× with no accuracy loss; Section 6.2 reports MBB final compliance within 1.5% of standard TO, but the timed 10-million-element comparison has no explicit matched-quality tolerance or equal-budget test.

R2.evidence: Sections 6 and 6.4: baseline uses the group's C++/CUDA FEA on the same machine and FEA GPU class as the ML run; no protocol weakness criterion is established.

R3.evidence: Sections 6.1 and 6.4: four conventional TO problems generate training data, but neither their runtime nor model training time nor break-even uses are reported; 26.5× covers optimization runs after offline training.

R4.evidence: Sections 6.2–6.3: physical compliance and volume are assessed for MBB designs and disconnected members are discussed qualitatively; no failure rate is counted, and 38-million-element bridge compliance is estimated from a coarse mesh.

reporting.n_test_cases: MBB beam and bridge families; multiple MBB mesh, volume and filter settings (Sections 6.2–6.3)

notes: Full text read from author-hosted version of record via web PDF viewer; direct download returned HTTP 403, without bypass. Figure 16 holds plotted timing rather than tabulated exact times.
